AM-T650 · whole-body DIRECT · flight test 2026-09-03 10:16

Why the whole-body hold diverged after the arm moved forward

Sources: whole_body_test_20260903_101609 (ROS bag) and log_321_2026-9-3-10-14-24.ulg (PX4). All times below are bag seconds; the PX4 log runs 20.47 s ahead.

Verdict. The vehicle diverged in a 0.33 Hz pitch-and-forward oscillation, which is exactly the natural frequency of the whole-body CoM position loop. The loop lost its damping because the attitude loop it commands through is too slow: at 0.33 Hz the attitude loop lags 64° and passes only 58% of the commanded tilt, which cancels the 57° of phase lead the velocity term provides. Net effective damping was slightly negative. The margin was already near zero in yesterday's flights; extending the arm added enough coupling and torque error to push it over.

Of the three hypotheses: gains are the primary cause, arm torque fidelity is a real amplifier from about 33 s on, and the disturbance estimator is not the driver. The same gains flew in simulation because the law's attitude feedforward makes the tilt follow its command almost perfectly when the model is exact; on hardware the bag shows the tilt following with the feedback-only response, so the feedforward was not delivering.

The oscillation is the position loop with no damping

The whole-body law sets the CoM force as f = −kxex − kvėx + mg − d̂. With kx = 16 N/m and m = 3.75 kg the loop's natural frequency is 2.07 rad/s, or 0.33 Hz, and the design damping ratio is 0.77. The measured oscillation period was 3.0 s. That coincidence is the first clue: a position loop ringing at its own natural frequency has lost its damping.

Where did the damping go? The force the law asks for is realized by tilting the base, and the tilt comes from the attitude loop with kR = 2, kw = 1.5 over a design inertia of 0.117 kg·m². That is a 4.1 rad/s loop with damping ratio 1.55, overdamped and only twice the position loop's frequency. Its response at 2.07 rad/s is gain 0.58 at −64°. The velocity term gives the commanded force +57° of lead; passing through the attitude loop leaves −7°. The realized force is then almost pure stiffness, 17 N/m, with a small negative damping component.

The bag confirms this directly. Reconstructing the horizontal thrust force from the PX4 attitude and the commanded collective, and comparing it with the logged CoM error:

Quantity at 0.33 HzPredicted from gainsMeasured 29–40 s
Realized force vs −ex17 N/m at −7°16.5 N/m at −11°
Realized force vs commanded force0.58 at −64°0.53 at −60°
Slowest closed-loop pole (real part)+0.14 to +0.34 s⁻¹+0.26 s⁻¹

The linear cascade with the flown gains is unstable even before any actuator delay, and the growth rate matches the flight. Yesterday's three flights ran the same gains: the fit on those bags gives the same near-zero phase and a 19–22 cm rms wander around the hold. The system was marginal then, not stable.

Your three hypotheses against the data

Primary
3. Gains. The attitude loop bandwidth is too close to the position loop bandwidth. This is the same cascade problem the classic AM DIRECT node hit and fixed by lowering kpos, recorded in the repo's notes. Here the fix can go either way: a faster attitude loop or a softer position loop.
Amplifier
2. Arm torque fidelity. Over the whole DIRECT window joint 2 delivered 67% of the commanded torque and joint 3 delivered 54%, with RMSE of 0.372 and 0.239 N·m. The shortfall is not uniform: it is under 3% below 1 N·m and reaches 67% above 2 N·m, and it scales with joint speed through back-EMF. The law pre-compensates the arm reaction in the base torque assuming the commanded joint torque is applied, so every unrealized newton-metre becomes a spurious pitch torque of the same order as the whole base pitch command, which is 0.95 N·m RMS. That accelerated the last cycles. But growth began at 28 s with commands the arm was still tracking to within 13%, so it is not the trigger. The section below audits every joint.
Not the cause
1. Disturbance model / L1. The momentum observer runs at 0.5 rad/s on translation and 0.1 rad/s on rotation and joints. Its oscillatory content at 0.33 Hz is 0.33 N rms, lagging about 180°, against force swings of ±13 N. It neither drove nor could have caught the oscillation. Its slowness does explain the 45 cm excursion on DIRECT entry and the steady −3 N x-bias, which matches the 4.8° nose-down hover pitch seen in SAFETY: the thrust axis and the IMU's level disagree by about 5°. A faster estimator would improve entry transients, but no estimator fixes a phase problem inside the cascade.

Did every joint execute its command torque?

Yes while it is nearly still, and no once it moves — and the boundary is sharp enough to write down. Across both flights the servo's command chain is reproduced from the logged torque to better than 0.25 duty counts, so what each motor was told to do is known exactly and the whole gap sits between that and what it did. At rest joints 2 and 3 deliver 99–100% and 94–98% of the commanded torque. In motion they lose a fixed 0.93 N·m (joint 2) and 1.49 N·m (joint 3) for every rad/s of joint speed, whatever the command is, until the loss exceeds the command and the motor brakes instead of pushing. That is one term, it is back-EMF, and the last section writes it out with constants you can paste into Isaac.

Joints 1 and 4 are a different case and not a measurement: their commanded torque — 0.04 and 0.03 N·m rms — never leaves the current sensor's own noise floor, so no delivery figure for them is worth quoting.

Three signals, and the equations that connect them

Everything below is in the arm's own sign convention, the one the servos see. Your model convention is τmodel = s ⊙ τarm with s = [−1, +1, +1, −1]; the flight node applies that flip before publishing, so no conversion happens anywhere in this section.

1 · Command torque — what the whole-body law asked for

τcmd,i = law_debug[9+i] ≡ joint_torque_command.effort[i]  [N·m]

The law's joint torque as the arm controller received it, already carrying the flight node's own ±3.0 N·m clamp. Logged on the arm's 250 Hz clock, which is why it is used here in preference to the command topic.

2 · Servo goal — what the motor was told to do

dutyi = law_debug[13+i]  [PWM counts, full scale 885]

The value written to the Dynamixel Goal PWM register. The servos ran in PWM mode (Operating Mode 16), so this is a voltage command, not a current one — that single fact is the origin of everything in this section.

3 · Applied torque — what the motor actually produced

τapp,i = joint_states.effort[i] / Ni  [N·m]

joint_states.effort is the servo's Present Current register (126) in raw signed ticks, and Ni is the per-joint torque constant from the arm repo's 2026-08-17 calibration campaign — [160, 173.8, 146.7, 160] counts/N·m. This is the motor's electromagnetic torque; it is not a torque-sensor reading and it does not include gearbox friction.

The chain from 1 to 2 is a pure unit conversion plus one feedforward, and both halves are recoverable from the logs:

dutyi = clip±885[  clip±dutymax,i( τcmd,i · Ni ρi )  +  semf · (885 · Ke,i / Vs) · q̇ref,i  ]

ρi = 885 · Ri · ILSB / Vs   [duty counts per current count]

equivalently dutyi = τcmd,i · PWMfull · Ri / (Kt,i · Vs), with Kt,i = 1/(Ni · ILSB). The second term is the controller's back-EMF feedforward: it is driven by the reference velocity q̇ref, added after the torque clamp, and scaled by back_emf_ff_scale = 1.0.

Every number in the right-hand four columns is recovered from the flight logs, not read out of a file — the duty caps in particular are identified as the exact saturation levels of the logged duty command.

The chain equation is exact. Over the 2 Sep flight — 24 287 DIRECT samples, no saturation, no joint outside its software limits — the largest disagreement between the logged duty and the equation above is 0.003 / 0.049 / 0.226 / 0.004 counts on joints 1 to 4. The worst of those, joint 3, is 1.8 mN·m. On 3 Sep it holds to 0.16 counts until 36.71 s, when joint 2 crosses its +50° software limit and the controller correctly substitutes its position-limit PD pull-back for the law's command; that is the only departure in either flight, it lasts 130 samples, and it is a designed behaviour rather than a defect.

What the arm controller adds to your torque — and what it added here

The controller can add six terms between your law and the servo. In command (duty-count) units, applied in this order, they are:

ui = τcmd,i · Ni ρi

ui += ( fi + λi · |garm,i(q)| ) · tanh( q̇ref,i / w )

Coulomb friction, friction_ff, friction_load_coeff, w = friction_ff_width

ui += vi · q̇ref,i

viscous friction, viscous_ff

ui += εi(t),  ε̇i = sgn(q̇ref,i) · ri while the joint is stuck, capped

breakaway/stiction escape, stiction_ramp_rate, stiction_ff

ui += Ai · sin(2π fd t)  if |q̇ref,i| > 0.005 and |q̇i| < gate

dither, dither_amplitude, dither_frequency_hz

ui += Ii(t),  İi = kI,i · (qref,i − qi), clamped

integral, ki, i_clamp

ui ← clip( ui, ±dutymax,i )

ui += semf · (PWMfull Ke,i / Vs) · q̇ref,i

back-EMF feedforward, after the clamp

In these two flights only the first and last of those were non-zero. That is not read from a config file, it is what the residual says: subtract the conversion and the back-EMF feedforward from the logged duty and what is left is at most 0.23 counts over 32 700 samples. A Coulomb term would show as a 4.7-count step on joint 2 and 7.8 on joint 3 each time the reference moved; the dither would show as a 48-count, 100 Hz ripple; the integral would show as a slow drift up to 57 counts. None of them is present at even 1% of those sizes. Adding the Coulomb term to the model makes the residual worse — 0.003 → 0.67 counts on joint 2 — which is how you can tell it was configured to zero rather than merely gated off.

This matters more than it looks. Every friction, stiction and dither term the arm controller owns is driven by the reference velocity q̇ref, and so is the back-EMF feedforward. Which term supplied what, and when, is decomposed from the logs in its own section below. In whole-body DIRECT the streamed reference holds the arm almost perfectly still — peak |q̇ref| was 0.009 rad/s on joint 2 and 0.20 rad/s on joint 3 — while the joints themselves reached 2.36 and 1.57 rad/s. So the one compensation that would have cancelled the loss described below was, by construction, asleep exactly when it was needed: it compensates the velocity the arm was asked to have, not the velocity it had.

The percentage curve

A single-sample ratio τapp/τcmd is meaningless wherever the command passes through zero, which on a hold is most of the time. The curve plotted under every torque trace below is the least-squares projection of delivered on commanded in a sliding ±1.0 s window:

η(t) = 100 · Σw τcmd τapp  /  Σw τcmd2  [%],   w = [t−1 s, t+1 s]

η = 100% means the motor produced exactly the torque the law asked for, on average over that second; η = 0 means it produced none of it; η < 0 means it produced torque in the opposite direction — it braked while the law was pushing. The curve is blank where the window carries less than 0.08 N·m rms of command, which is why joints 1 and 4 are mostly empty. Measured signals are advanced by one control cycle (4 ms) before comparison, so η scores amplitude and not transport delay.

Command against applied, joint by joint, for the whole 34.0 s of DIRECT. The dashed grey trace is the back-EMF model of the last section, evaluated from the logged duty and the logged joint speed with no fitted parameter. Phase bands are marked along the axis and named in the strip beneath; red phases are the ones where the vehicle was misbehaving, which — as the curves show — is not the same question as whether the joint was.

The raw curves — 2 Sep 12:46, the flight that behaved

Ninety-seven seconds of DIRECT with three commanded transitions and no oscillation at any point: roll stayed inside −1.6…+0.7° and pitch inside −8.3…−1.5° for the whole window. It is the control case for everything above, and it is the record that shows the delivery gap is not a symptom of the divergence. Traces are bin-averaged to 25 Hz here, the flight being three times as long.

The two other 2 Sep recordings carry no arm data

Worth stating so nobody scores them. In wb_tracking_20260902_125222 and …_125951 the joint state is bit-identical for the whole of DIRECT — positions frozen at 0.697961, 0.697961, 0.001534, 0.003068 rad and currents at 99, 33, 0, 0 counts across 500 and 21 499 messages whose header stamps advance normally. Real encoders jitter and real currents never repeat exactly, so the Dynamixel read path was dead in both. Neither flight can be used to judge torque tracking, and — more seriously — in both of them the whole-body law computed its arm dynamics from a constant arm state.

Read down the q̇ rms columns. Every one of the sixteen phase-joint cells with an rms speed under 0.04 rad/s delivered between 93 and 109% with a mean error of 0.045 N·m or less. Every cell above 0.12 rad/s carries a mean error between 0.15 and 1.03 N·m. The error scales with speed at roughly the coefficient b of the model below, in both flights, and the vehicle's own health does not enter — the 2 Sep flight was calm throughout and its joint 3 still lost 0.17 N·m in each of its first two transitions.

Two things this table rules out. Saturation is not the mechanism: the duty command never reached its cap in any phase of either flight except the last 4.6 s of 3 Sep, by which time delivery had been failing for twelve seconds. And η alone is not a sufficient test — the commanded torque carries a large static gravity-hold component (0.5–0.8 N·m on joint 2), which the motor does deliver, so the projection can read 104% in a phase whose mean error is already 0.040 N·m. Read η and the mean error together, or read the model.

The six extra terms, and what each contributed

The sum of the six needs no assumption — it is the logs, directly. Subtract the clamped unit conversion from the duty the controller wrote and what is left is the extra terms:

Δτff(t) = [ duty − clip±dutymax( τcmd · N · ρ ) ] / (N · ρ)   [N·m]

Plotted against the droop those terms exist to cancel, b·q̇. On 3 Sep the curve is drawn only to 36.5 s: past that joint 2 crosses its software limit and the controller substitutes its PD pull-back for the law's command, so the difference above stops being "the extra terms" and the decomposition is meaningless.

Which term supplied it

Fitting the six basis functions to Δτff over the clean, unsaturated, in-range samples gives one non-zero coefficient. The bars are linear, as a share of joint 3's total:

termdriven bycontribution, 3 Sepjoint 2joint 3

rms contribution in mN·m over the decomposition window (7388 samples per joint), and the bar is that as a fraction of joint 3's total. The dotted mark sits at one Dynamixel current tick — 6.82 mN·m, 9.6% of the total — the finest torque the servo can even report. Every term except the back-EMF feedforward is three to four decades below that mark (their bars are drawn at a minimum width so the rows stay readable; the true values are in the columns). That is the measurement saying they were configured off, not merely gated off.

Two details worth stating rather than hiding:

  • Viscous friction cannot be separated from the back-EMF feedforward. Both are exactly proportional to q̇ref, so no fit can tell them apart in the unsaturated regime (they differ only in that one is applied before the torque clamp and the other after). What is measurable is their sum, and it comes out at 210.94 and 177.00 duty counts per rad/s against a configured 885·Ke/Vs of 210.92 and 177.00. The back-EMF term alone accounts for the total to five figures, so the viscous coefficient is zero to the precision of the fit.
  • The residual is 0.02–0.32 mN·m rms. Whatever the other five terms did, it is smaller than a twentieth of a current tick.

And it fired at the wrong time

This is the part the totals hide. Every one of those six terms is driven by the arm controller's own reference velocity, and that reference is not synchronised with the whole-body trajectory. It is awake for only 14.1% of DIRECT on 3 Sep and 7.9% on 2 Sep — and in windows that follow the governor's transitions rather than coinciding with them:

Read the 2 Sep first row again: the reference sweeps at 0.2 rad/s for nearly four seconds while the joint moves one tenth of a degree. The whole-body law had already taken the arm to the goal; the arm controller's own min-jerk reference was still slewing toward a target that had been reached. Over the whole flight the reference travels 51.0° while the joint travels 288.1° — it accounts for 18% of the motion on 2 Sep and 16% on 3 Sep.

N·m rms		required

The pattern is exact and it is inverted: 0.0–1.3% in every phase where the arm was commanded to move, 144–223% in three phases where it was not. The compensation was not merely late — during the holds it over-supplied, injecting torque the joint had no droop to spend it on.

So it did not just fail to help — it made the disturbance larger. Correlate what the six terms supplied against the droop they had to cancel and you get +0.040 on 3 Sep and +0.066 on 2 Sep: essentially uncorrelated. A non-zero signal uncorrelated with its target does not subtract from it, it adds variance. Measured on joint 3, the variance of the uncancelled droop grew by 27.5% on 3 Sep and 57.1% on 2 Sep.

That is the whole feedforward story in one line: of six compensation terms, five were off, and the sixth was keyed to a reference that moved at the wrong times and by a sixth of the right amount.

Are the two reference chains synchronised?

No — and not by a little. There are two joint references in this stack and they run the same move one after the other:

the law's reference

qd(t)  ←  whole_body_direct_actuation/reference (WholeBodyReference)

What the governor plans and streams at 100 Hz, and what the whole-body law tracks. Model convention, mapped here to the arm's by s = [−1, +1, +1, −1].

the arm controller's reference

qcmd(t)  ←  external_torque_controller/smoothed_reference_joint_trajectory

The base class's own min-jerk reference. The law ignores it while the torque stream is fresh — but every one of the six compensation terms is keyed to it, and so is the stale-fallback PD hold and the DIRECT-entry gate.

The lag, per joint

Onset of each reference's motion, taken as the first sustained sample above 1 °/s:

flightjointgovernor q̇d movedarm q̇cmd movedlagpeak °/s

Three things fall out of that table, and the third is the one that matters.

  • The endpoints agree exactly. 8.28° and 8.28° on 3 Sep; 40.00° and 40.00° on 2 Sep. The arm controller is being told the right goal — it is the same number the governor solved. So this is a timing fault, not a wiring or convention fault.
  • The lag is the length of the move. 3.0 to 4.1 s, against governor moves of 2.4 to 3.0 s. The arm controller starts when the governor stops, which is the signature of a goal delivered once, at completion rather than streamed during the move.
  • Nothing in the bag carries that goal. external_torque_controller/target_joint_setpoint — the topic the governor's _arm_sync_tick publishes to at 20 Hz while EXECUTING — recorded zero messages in both flights, though the recorder was subscribed to it and the governor spent 3.9 s and 11.4 s in EXECUTING. So the goal reaches the arm controller by a path this recording is blind to.

    Corrected 2026-09-04. An earlier version of this section argued from rosbag2's offered_qos_profiles that the governor's publisher was not in the graph at all. That was wrong — a live capture of the same stack reads Publisher count: 2 on that topic (the governor's arm-sync and the arm ground station), and the metadata field is not a reliable publisher count. The publisher is there; what did not happen is the publishing.

Consequence. The compensation terms, the stale-fallback PD hold and the DIRECT-entry gate are all computed against a joint trajectory that is a delayed replay of one the vehicle already flew. That is why the back-EMF feedforward fires in the holds and sleeps through the transitions, and it is upstream of the choice between q̇ref and q̇meas — feeding the term measured velocity fixes what it compensates, but not the fact that the arm controller's picture of the arm is three seconds stale.

The rule, and a model you can put in Isaac

One sentence: in PWM mode the duty command is a voltage, so the torque the motor makes is the commanded torque minus a fixed amount per unit of joint speed. The winding sees V − Keq̇ across R, not V, and the current — hence the torque — falls by KtKeq̇/R no matter what was asked for. Everything measured in this report is that one term.

The other cells have too few samples above 0.15 rad/s to fit. η at rest is the projection over samples below 0.005 rad/s carrying more than 0.2 N·m of command.

Two readings of that table. First, Kt2/R predicts the measurement with no free parameter — 0.934 against 0.950 on joint 2 and 1.493 against a two-flight mean of 1.443 on joint 3. It has to: for any DC machine Ke = Kt in SI units, so the one calibrated constant you already have fixes the droop as well as the torque. Substituting it into the time series turns the model error into 0.134 N·m rms on 3 Sep joint 2 against 0.247 for an ideal joint, and 0.067 against 0.222 on joint 3 — the same value an individually fitted coefficient reaches.

Second, and worth acting on: the controller's configured back_emf_ke[2] = 2.86 is inconsistent with joint 2's own calibrated Kt = 2.139, by 34%. It was not exercised in these flights because the reference velocity that drives it stayed near zero, but any future run that does move the reference will over-compensate joint 2 by a third. The values implied by the torque calibration are [2.323, 2.139, 2.534, 2.323].

The rules, stated so they can be checked

  1. At rest the arm is an honest torque source. Below 0.005 rad/s joints 2 and 3 deliver 99–100% and 94–98% of the command, over 20 000 samples. Nothing in the gearbox, the calibration or the transport needs fixing.
  2. The loss is a fixed torque per unit speed, not a percentage. Δτ = −b·(q̇ − semfq̇ref), with b = 0.93 N·m/(rad/s) on joint 2 and 1.49 on joint 3, independent of how much torque was asked for.
  3. Hence the percentage delivered is a property of the command, not of the motor: η = 1 − b|q̇|/|τ|. Ninety percent delivery therefore requires |τcmd| ≥ 10·b·|q̇|, and the torque reverses sign at |q̇| = |τcmd|/b.

Against that table, the 3 Sep flight asked joint 2 for 3.0 N·m while it was moving at 2.36 rad/s — a loss of 2.20 N·m, which is more than the joint's entire 2.16 N·m duty ceiling — and joint 3 for 3.0 N·m at 1.57 rad/s, a loss of 2.35 N·m against a 1.53 N·m ceiling. In the last four seconds neither joint could have delivered its command by any margin of tuning.

The model, for Isaac Sim

Four lines, one array of constants, no fitting. Apply it wherever 06_px4_direct_t650_aerial_manipulator_ros2_arm_torque.py currently writes the commanded effort straight through:

NM2C = np.array([160.0, 173.8, 146.7, 160.0])   # counts/N.m, 2026-08-17 calibration
R    = np.array([4.90, 4.90, 4.30, 4.90])       # motor_resistance_ohm
KT   = 1.0 / (NM2C * 0.00269)                   # -> [2.323, 2.139, 2.534, 2.323] N.m/A
B    = KT ** 2 / R                              # -> [1.102, 0.934, 1.493, 1.102] N.m/(rad/s)
TAU_MAX = np.array([0.370, 2.160, 1.535, 0.370])  # duty ceiling as flown

def applied_torque(tau_cmd, qd, qd_ref=0.0, s_emf=1.0):
    """OM-X XM430 in PWM mode: a voltage source, not a torque source."""
    tau = np.clip(tau_cmd, -TAU_MAX, TAU_MAX)
    return tau - B * (qd - s_emf * qd_ref)

qd_ref is the arm controller's own reference velocity, which is what its back-EMF feedforward cancels; pass the streamed qdot_d if you want to reproduce the real stack, or leave it at zero, which is what these two flights effectively did. If you want the duty ceiling exactly, clamp in duty counts — N·ρ·τ against [57.6, 364.9, 192.0, 57.6] — because the feedforward is added after that clamp and can push the total to the ±885 PWM full scale.

What this model does not include

  • Joints 1 and 4 are unverified. Their commands never left the current sensor's noise floor, and on the little that is measurable the model over-predicts — joint 1's fitted 0.457 against a theoretical 1.102, at R² 0.50. Use Kt2/R for them, since it is the same machine, but do not treat it as measured.
  • τapp is electromagnetic torque, not link torque. It is Kt × Present Current, so it counts what the motor makes and not what survives the 353:1 gearbox. The real link sees this minus Coulomb and viscous friction, which the flight data cannot separate because there is no torque sensor. A model built on this alone still over-states what reaches the arm.
  • No gearbox friction, and the flight data cannot supply it. What the transitions leave behind is a tracking lag, not a standing offset: against the streamed qd, joint 3 trails by 6–10° through every commanded transition in both flights and then closes to under 2° during the hold that follows — +6.2° → +1.9° and −7.0° → +0.3° on 2 Sep. An error that disappears when the joint stops is the signature of a speed-dependent loss, which is reassuring for this model and is also why the model cannot see stiction: any static friction is hidden inside the same 0.02 N·m residual as the sensor noise. If your Isaac arm needs a breakaway torque, it has to come from a bench measurement, not from these bags.
  • The fix removes the term rather than modelling it. In current-control mode (Operating Mode 0) the servo closes its own loop on the current, R and Ke drop out, and b goes to zero. If the arm moves to current control, this model should be deleted, not retuned.

Method. Bags read with rosbag2's sqlite store and deserialized with rclpy; all times are bag receive time minus the bag's first message, one clock (hardware). Torque signals are put on a common 250 Hz grid by linear interpolation over the DIRECT window, with the measured side advanced one control cycle so amplitude rather than transport delay is scored. Delivered torque is the Dynamixel Present Current register through the arm repo's 2026-08-17 per-joint constants; the servo goal is the logged Goal PWM count through the identified duty-per-N·m map. The six extra terms are decomposed by projecting the measured duty residual onto each term's own basis function over the unsaturated, in-limit samples. Scripts and the extracted arrays are in docs/experimental_data_ros2_bag/0903 - T650-AM whole-body/analysis/ (extract_wb_bag_0903.py, applied_torque_analysis.py).
